title: Pages need a level-one heading
summary: The page has no h1, so people who navigate by headings have no clear starting point. Add one h1 that names what the page is about.
problem: The page has no <h1> element. Headings give a page its outline, and the h1 is the title of that outline: it tells a visitor what this page is about before they read anything else.
whoItAffects: Screen reader users often move through a page by jumping between headings, and an h1 gives them a clear place to start. Without one they have to listen from the top to work out where they are. Search engines also use headings to understand a page's topic.
steps: Decide what the page is about and put that in one short heading, such as the product name or the article title.
Mark it up as an h1 inside the main content area, before any other headings.
If your design already shows a large title in a div or span, change that element to an h1 and keep the look with CSS.
Use h2 to h6 for the sections below it, in order, and check that every page type in your theme or template outputs its h1.
before:
Spring sale

Free delivery on raised beds until the end of May.
after:
Spring sale

Free delivery on raised beds until the end of May.
whyItMatters: Without an h1, assistive technology users and search engines both have a harder time telling what the page is for. This is a best practice rather than a WCAG failure, but a clear title heading is one of the cheapest structure fixes you can make.
howToCheck: Search the page source for <h1, or use your browser's accessibility inspector to view the heading outline. There should be one h1, near the top of the main content.

platformNotes.note: Most themes print the page or post title as an h1. If yours does not, edit the theme template that outputs the title so it is wrapped in an h1.
